title: The silence of God
hookLine: Psalm 22 and the cross both hold God's silence

lines: I CRY IN THE DAY TIME.
cards: "O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent."
That's the second verse of Psalm twenty-two, a song addressed to the chief musician, set down by someone who has called out day and night and heard nothing back.
Some people live that line long before they find it in the Bible: the phone that doesn't ring, the prayer that seems to hit the ceiling. And this is the psalm Jesus reaches for on the cross.

teach.b: Year two had a psalm about waiting in silence. This silence is harder. The psalm names it honestly.
It doesn't pretend God answered: thou hearest not. And that line was kept in the Psalms, to be prayed instead of hidden. Then the cross.
Matthew records Jesus crying out, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those are the opening words of this same psalm.

teach.h: ELI, ELI: NO VOICE FROM HEAVEN.
teach.b: At his baptism, Matthew says, a voice spoke from heaven. Here, the Gospel records no voice in reply. Only the cry, and soon after, his death.

teach.h: THE SAME PSALM TURNS: HE HEARD.
teach.b: Christians have read this moment in different ways: some hear Jesus truly feeling abandoned; others note he's praying a psalm that turns to trust. Some hold both. And the psalm does turn.
Further on it says God "hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard."
The psalm that began with thou hearest not comes round to he heard. For the psalmist, silence wasn't the same as absence. Last, a day of silence on the calendar.

teach.h: HOLY SATURDAY: A DAY OF WAITING.
teach.b: Between Good Friday and Easter morning comes Holy Saturday. In some churches the altar is stripped bare and the bells stay quiet. Nothing is announced.

The body lies in the tomb. Lamentations has a line for days like that: "It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD." The churches that mark it keep that waiting on purpose.

how: Some churches read Psalm 22 in Holy Week, and on Holy Saturday some churches strip the altar, silence the bells and hold no ordinary service until the Easter Vigil, keeping the day as one of waiting.

games.q: what does “the silence of god” mean?
o: a stretch when prayer seems to meet no answer at all
proof that God has turned away from someone for good
a monk's vow to stop speaking for a holy season

games.q: the silence of God — tap the pairs.
p: I cry, but thou hearest not
when he cried unto him, he heard
my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me
the bells quiet, the altar bare

s: Jesus's cry from the cross comes from a psalm
my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me opens Psalm 22.
Matthew records a voice from heaven at Jesus's baptism, and none in reply at the cross
at the baptism a voice speaks; at the cross there is only the cry, and then his death.
the Bible hides the moments when God seems silent
Psalm 22 says it plainly: thou hearest not.

games.q: you're standing near the cross, and you hear Jesus cry out: Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani. what are those words?
o: a new prayer no one had heard before.
the opening of Psalm 22: my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
words with no meaning at all.
games.why: Matthew gives the cry as the opening of Psalm 22, a psalm that says thou hearest not and later turns to he heard. Jesus prays the silence in the psalm's own words.

practice: Let the room go quiet, with no music, no words, no list, and if a question has been sitting in you without an answer, let it be there, unanswered. Notice that silence has a texture: a hum, a breath, a car far away.
If you pray, wait before God without saying anything at all; if you don't, wait anyway, and let the quiet be enough.

wordCard.voice: The silence of God. The stretch when prayer seems to meet nothing, prayed in Psalm twenty-two and on the cross, and kept each year on Holy Saturday.

orig.note: Hebrew: my God, the first word of Psalm 22, which Matthew gives on Jesus's lips as Eli.

carryVoice: Your line: silence is not absence. Holy Saturday still comes before Easter morning. Until tomorrow.
